sections.title: Enterprise Network Architecture
sections.content:
ARCHITECTURE AND INFRASTRUCTURE CONCEPTS
• Network infrastructure — media, appliances, addressing/forwarding protocols supporting connectivity
• Network applications — services running on infrastructure for business activity
• Data assets — information created/stored/transferred by business activity
Example: email requires access control at the client, a mailbox server (confidentiality + availability), and a mail transfer server (mediates untrusted Internet traffic) — placing all three in one segment introduces avoidable vulnerabilities.
NETWORK INFRASTRUCTURE LAYER MODEL (OSI)
Layer | Function | Appliance/Protocol
1 (PHY) | Physical signal transmission | Cabling, radio
2 | MAC-address forwarding within a broadcast domain | Switches, wireless access points
3 | IP-address forwarding between networks | Routers
4 | Port-based session transport | TCP (reliable), UDP (connectionless)
7 (App) | Client/server user-level services | HTTP, email, file transfer, DNS
• Host node — initiates transfers (server/client); intermediary node — forwards traffic
• LAN — single-site scope; WAN — metro/country/global scope
• MAC address — 48-bit hex value (e.g. 00-15-5D-01-CA-4A), local-segment only
• ARP (IPv4) / ND (IPv6) — map IP address to MAC address
SWITCHING INFRASTRUCTURE
Structured cabling — wall port → patch panel → switch port, forming a star topology. All hosts on a switch share one broadcast domain — flat and insecure at scale (any host can freely try to reach any other).
Hierarchical design — access switches serve blocks of hosts; routers interconnect blocks, creating separate broadcast domains and enabling a zone-based security model. A layer 3 switch combines routing + switching for the core layer.
ROUTING INFRASTRUCTURE (LAYER 3)
Concept | Detail
IPv4 | 32-bit, dotted decimal; /24 prefix or 255.255.255.0 mask splits network ID / host ID
IPv6 | 128-bit hex; last 64 bits = interface ID, first 64 bits = hierarchical network info
Subnet | A layer-3 broadcast domain within a larger network
VLAN | Switch-level segmentation feature; ID range 2–4,094; maps a physical switch port to a logical broadcast domain regardless of physical location; traffic between VLANs must be routed
SECURITY ZONES
Untrusted public Internet zone outside the perimeter; internal zones vary by trust/access needs:
Asset Type | Priority
Databases/file systems | Confidentiality + integrity — split across zones to limit breach impact
Client devices | Integrity + availability (lower confidentiality need — shouldn't store data)
Public-facing app servers | Integrity + availability — never fully trusted, shouldn't hold sensitive data
Infrastructure servers (auth, directory, monitoring) | High CIA across the board — compromise = catastrophic
Traffic between zones is controlled by a firewall, applying least privilege. A zone needs a known, single entry/exit point.
Example privilege-based access rules:
• Low-privilege zone (e.g. printers) — can accept, cannot initiate
• Enterprise LAN clients — can initiate outbound, cannot accept new inbound
• Guest zone — Internet only, no enterprise LAN access
• Public-facing servers — accept from Internet only, cannot initiate to LAN or Internet
• VLAN-level rules within a zone (e.g. app servers can query databases, not vice versa)
ATTACK SURFACE & WEAKNESSES
Layer-based attack surface: L1/2 (rogue physical/wireless connections), L3 (address spoofing across zones), L4/7 (unauthorized port/protocol access). Defense in depth = layered control categories/functions across all layers.
Weakness | Risk
Single points of failure | One appliance/link outage stops everything
Complex dependencies | One service failure cascades
Availability over confidentiality/integrity | "Quick fix" shortcuts create long-term risk
Lack of documentation/change control | Shadow IT, invisible drift
Overdependence on perimeter security | Flat internal network = free lateral movement post-breach
PORT SECURITY
Physical switch access should be restricted (locked rooms/cabinets); disabling unused ports or removing patch cables has overhead and can be bypassed.
Method | Description
MAC Filtering/Limiting | Port allows only a list or a capped number of MAC addresses
802.1X (PNAC) | Requires authentication before granting full port access
802.1X AAA roles:
Role | Function
Supplicant | Device requesting access
Authenticator | Switch/access point — conduit only, doesn't validate
Authentication Server | Validates credentials, issues authorizations, does accounting
• EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) — framework for pluggable auth methods, often paired with certs
• RADIUS — carries auth/authz decisions between authenticator (RADIUS client) and authentication server (RADIUS server)
• Port opens only for EAPoL until authenticated; full access granted after RADIUS confirms
PHYSICAL ISOLATION
Air-gapped host/network — no physical or wireless connection to any other network (e.g., root CA, malware analysis box, military/government/industrial sites). Improves security but complicates administration (local terminal only; USB/optical media updates — itself an attack vector requiring scanning).
ARCHITECTURE CONSIDERATIONS
Factor | Consideration
Cost | Capital outlay + ongoing maintenance vs. reduced incident losses
Compute/Responsiveness | CPU/memory/storage/bandwidth sized to workload
Scalability/Ease of Deployment | Ability to add/remove capacity without excess cost
Availability | Minimize downtime (planned + unplanned)
Resilience/Ease of Recovery | Time and manual effort to recover from failure
Power | Facility capacity to meet device/workload energy demands
Patch Availability | Ability to patch — limited when relying on a third party or EOL products
Risk Transference | Contracting a third party under an SLA with penalties for missed metrics
On-premises networks: high capital cost, low scalability, complex large-scale disaster recovery — lower availability/resilience than cloud alternatives.

sections.title: Network Security Appliances
sections.content:
DEVICE PLACEMENT — DEFENSE IN DEPTH
Control Type | Typical Placement
Preventive | Segment/zone border (firewalls); load balancers ensure availability
Detective | Within the perimeter, monitoring internal traffic that evaded border controls
Preventive + Detective + Corrective | Host-level endpoint protection (firewall, A-V, IDS, DLP)
DEVICE ATTRIBUTES
Attribute Pair | Meaning
Active vs. Passive | Passive: no client/agent config, undetectable, e.g. traffic copied to a sensor. Active: requires credentials/config/agent, e.g. a scanning tool or a gateway filter
Inline vs. Tap/Monitor | Inline: part of the cable path, no IP/MAC needed on the device. SPAN/mirror port: switch copies frames to a sensor (can drop errored/overloaded frames). TAP: physical inductor/optical splitter copies every frame regardless of load — more reliable
Fail-Open vs. Fail-Closed | Fail-open: preserves access, favors availability, risks engineered failure abuse. Fail-closed: blocks access, favors confidentiality/integrity, risks downtime
Failure causes: power/hardware fault, software bug/vulnerability, config error (human factors), natural disaster.
FIREWALLS
Packet filtering — rules (ACL) match packet headers:
Filter Type | Basis
IP filtering | Source/destination IP (or MAC)
Protocol ID/type | TCP, UDP, ICMP, routing protocols
Port filtering | Source/destination TCP/UDP port
Action | Result
Accept/Permit | Packet passes
Drop/Deny | Silently discarded
Reject | Blocked + ICMP error sent to sender
Separate ACLs for inbound/outbound; outbound filtering blocks unauthorized apps and malware (e.g. backdoors).
Appliance firewall deployment modes:
Mode | Layer | Addressing
Routed | 3 | Each interface has IP + MAC, forwards between subnets
Bridged | 2 | MAC only, bridges two nodes (e.g. router + switch) — "transparent"
Inline | 1 | No MAC/IP at all — "virtual wire"/"bump-in-the-wire" — "transparent"
Transparent modes avoid re-addressing existing infrastructure but need a separate management interface. A router firewall bundles filtering into router firmware (routing is primary; SOHO routers are the classic example).
Stateless vs. Stateful:
• Stateless — evaluates each packet independently; least processing but weak against multi-packet attacks, awkward with load balancing/dynamic ports
• Stateful inspection — tracks sessions in a state table; new connections get full rule evaluation, established ones pass with less overhead
Layer 4 Firewall | Layer 7 Firewall
Examines TCP handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK), sequence numbers; flags anomalies as flooding/hijacking; can track UDP (harder) and ICMP anomalies | Inspects headers + payload; verifies protocol matches port (blocks malware disguising traffic as port 80); AKA application layer gateway, stateful multilayer inspection, deep packet inspection
PROXY SERVERS
Store-and-forward model: deconstruct → analyze → rebuild → forward.
Type | Direction | Notes
Forward Proxy | Outbound | Client → Internet (e.g. web proxy on TCP 80/443); provides caching + traffic control
Reverse Proxy | Inbound | Internet client → internal app server, typically at the network edge into a screened subnet
Proxy Mode | Client Awareness
Non-transparent | Client configured with proxy address/port (conventionally TCP/8080)
Transparent (forced/intercepting) | Intercepts without client reconfiguration; implemented as router or inline appliance
PAC (Proxy Auto-Configuration) script + WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-discovery) — automate client proxy configuration.
INTRUSION DETECTION / PREVENTION
System | Behavior
IDS | Passive — sensor (SPAN/TAP) feeds an analysis engine (Snort, Suricata, Zeek/Bro); alerts/logs on signature match, does not block; undetectable, no latency added
IPS | Active — can shun (block source, temp/permanent), reset the connection, or redirect to a honeypot/honeynet
NEXT-GENERATION FIREWALLS (NGFW) & UTM
NGFW (2010, Palo Alto) typically adds: L7 app-aware filtering (incl. TLS inspection), directory integration for per-user/role/time policies, IPS functionality, cloud integration.
UTM (Unified Threat Management) — centralizes firewall, antimalware, IPS, spam/content filtering, DLP, VPN, cloud access gateway, endpoint scanning into one appliance/console.
| NGFW | UTM
Focus | Fewer features, better performance | "Do everything" turnkey
Best fit | Enterprise | Small/medium business, limited IT resources
Risk | — | Single point of failure; possible latency under load
LOAD BALANCERS
Distributes requests across a server farm/pool for scalability, DoS mitigation, and fault tolerance.
Type | Basis
Layer 4 | IP + TCP/UDP port
Layer 7 (content switch) | Application data — URL, content type (video/audio)
• Scheduling — round robin (simplest), fewest connections, best response time; can be weighted; verified via heartbeat/health checks
• Source IP affinity — layer 4, client "stuck" to the node that accepted the first request
• Session persistence — layer 7, uses a cookie (set by node or injected by balancer) — more reliable but requires cookie support
WEB APPLICATION FIREWALLS (WAF)
Protects web servers/back-end databases from code injection and DoS; uses signatures/pattern matching on app-layer traffic; deployed as an appliance or a web-server plug-in; findings go to a log.

sections.title: Secure Communications
sections.content:
REMOTE ACCESS ARCHITECTURE
VPN Topology | Use Case
Client-to-site (remote access) | "Telecommuter" model — client-initiated connection to a VPN gateway
Site-to-site | Automatic, gateway-to-gateway trust relationship; hosts unaware of the VPN
Host-to-host | Secures traffic between two computers over an untrusted network
Legacy PPTP is deprecated (inadequate security). Preferred: TLS and IPsec.
TLS VPN
Client connects via digital certificate (server cert always; client cert optional for mutual authentication). Creates an encrypted tunnel for credential submission (often via RADIUS). Can run over TCP or UDP (DTLS = TLS over UDP, better for latency-sensitive voice/video). Use TLS 1.3 (1.2 still acceptable); earlier versions deprecated.
IPSEC VPN
Protocol | Function
AH (Authentication Header) | Hashes whole packet + shared secret → ICV; integrity only, no encryption
ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) | Encrypts payload; adds header, trailer, ICV; excludes IP header from the ICV calc
Mode | Use Case | Behavior
Transport | Host-to-host on a private network | Only payload encrypted (with ESP); AH can protect the IP header's integrity
Tunnel | Site-to-site over an untrusted network | Whole original packet encrypted + encapsulated with a new IP header (ESP); AH has no real tunnel-mode use case
IKE (Internet Key Exchange) — negotiates the security association (SA): authentication method, mutually supported ciphers, key exchange.
IKE Phase | Task
Phase I | Diffie-Hellman key agreement + peer identity, via digital certificates or a pre-shared key
Phase II | Negotiates ciphers/key sizes for AH/ESP within the Phase I secure channel
IKEv2 advantages over v1: supports EAP (e.g. RADIUS user auth), simpler low-bandwidth setup mode, NAT traversal, and MOBIKE multihoming (keeps tunnel alive across Wi-Fi/cellular switches).
REMOTE DESKTOP
Graphical remote access sends screen/audio to client, keyboard/mouse back to host.
Tool | Notes
RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) | Microsoft, encrypted by default, one-to-one machine access; remote desktop gateway for virtual desktops/apps
TeamViewer / VNC | Cross-platform alternatives
HTML5 VPN / clientless remote desktop gateway | Browser-only via canvas element + WebSocket (e.g. Apache Guacamole)
SECURE SHELL (SSH)
Primary secure CLI remote access + secure file transfer (SFTP); most common implementation is OpenSSH. Server identified by a public/private host key (must be rotated if host compromise is suspected — an attacker with the private key can spoof the server).
Client authentication methods (configured in /etc/ssh/sshd_config):
Method | Mechanism
Username/password | Verified locally or via RADIUS
Public key authentication | Client's public key added to server's authorized list
Kerberos | Client submits TGT via GSSAPI; server validates against the Ticket Granting Service
Common commands: `` ssh bobby@10.1.0.10 ssh-keygen -t rsa ssh-copy-id bobby@10.1.0.10 scp bobby@10.1.0.10:/logs/audit.log audit.log `` Delete a user's public key from the server immediately if their private key is compromised or access is revoked.
OUT-OF-BAND MANAGEMENT & JUMP SERVERS
Concept | Description
In-band management | Shares the production network; must use TLS/IPsec/RDP/SSH encryption
Out-of-band (OOB) management | Serial console/modem port, or a physically/VLAN-separated management network — costlier but preserves access during production outages, more secure
Jump Server | Single hardened admin server in a secure zone running only necessary admin protocols (SSH/RDP); target servers' ACLs allow only the jump server, reducing attack surface for managing many hosts
SAW (Secure Administrative Workstation) — locked-down client for admin channels only; minimal software, restricted/no Internet access, strict auditing.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Identify business workflows and their servers/clients/protocols/data assets; design segmented zones/blocks using VLANs, subnets, and firewall policies.
• Deploy switching and routing to support each block, applying port security or 802.1X NAC.
• Analyze the attack surface and select effective controls:
• Port security or 802.1X NAC against rogue device attachment.
• Routing firewalls for zone-perimeter access control and intrusion prevention (layer 4 or 7).
• Transparent firewalls to protect hosts/segments without re-addressing.
• IDS sensors behind firewalls or on mirrored ports to monitor intra-zone traffic.
• Proxy servers, NGFW, and WAF for advanced application/user-aware filtering.
• UTM where consolidated security capability alongside firewall/IPS is needed.
• Design load-balanced services for high availability and fault tolerance.
• Accommodate client-to-site, site-to-site, and host-to-host remote access with TLS and IPsec VPN protocols.
• Implement RDP and SSH for secure desktop/shell remote access; use a jump server to consolidate management of servers in a protected zone.

practice_questions.q: In an IaaS cloud model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
practice_questions.explanation: Under the shared responsibility model, IaaS customers manage the OS and above.

practice_questions.q: Which device sits between a trusted internal network and the internet and filters traffic based on rules?
practice_questions.explanation: Firewalls enforce traffic rules at network boundaries.

practice_questions.q: A company uses a SaaS email platform. Who is mainly responsible for securing the application code?
practice_questions.explanation: In SaaS the provider manages the application; the customer manages its data and access.

practice_questions.q: Public web servers are placed in a separate zone between the internet and the internal LAN. What is this zone called?
practice_questions.explanation: A screened subnet isolates public-facing servers.

practice_questions.q: Defining servers, networks and firewall rules in code files that can be versioned and redeployed is called:
practice_questions.explanation: IaC manages infrastructure through code for consistency.

practice_questions.q: An administrator connects to a hardened server first, and only from there reaches sensitive internal servers. What is that first server called?
practice_questions.explanation: A jump server is a controlled gateway for administrative access.

practice_questions.q: Which architecture runs code only when an event triggers it, with the provider managing the servers?
practice_questions.explanation: Serverless functions run on demand without customers managing servers.

practice_questions.q: Which device inspects traffic and actively blocks attacks it detects, sitting inline?
practice_questions.explanation: An IPS is inline and can block; an IDS only alerts.

practice_questions.q: An application split into many small, independent services that communicate through APIs is called:
practice_questions.explanation: Microservices break an app into independently deployable parts.

practice_questions.q: A device that spreads incoming web traffic across several servers improves which property?
practice_questions.explanation: Load balancers keep services available under load or when one server fails.
